
# Linear Regression Recap

## Single Linear Regression (SLR)

Scenario: use _head circumference (mm)_ to predict _age (weeks)_ of a fetal baby

$$
\boldsymbol{x} = \begin{pmatrix}
    105 \\
    120 \\
    110 \\
    117 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    20 \\
    24 \\
    22 \\
    23 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    20.3 \\
    24.0 \\
    21.5 \\
    23.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$\hat{y}(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$$

```{python}
circumference = np.array([[105], [120], [110], [117]])
age = np.array([20, 24, 22, 23])
model = LinearRegression().fit(circumference, age)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.4f}, Slope: {model.coef_[0]:.4f}")
model.predict(circumference)
```

## Mean squared error

$$
\boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    20 \\
    24 \\
    22 \\
    23 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    20.3 \\
    24.0 \\
    21.5 \\
    23.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} - \hat{\boldsymbol{y}}  = \begin{pmatrix}
    -0.3 \\
    0 \\
    0.5 \\
    -0.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-dpi: 300
predicted_age = model.predict(circumference)

x = circumference.flatten()
y = age
yhat = predicted_age
error = np.abs(y - yhat)
mse = np.mean(error ** 2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2), dpi=300)
ax.scatter(x, y, color="black", zorder=3)
order = np.argsort(x)
ax.plot(x[order], yhat[order], color="black")
for xi, yi, yhi, ei in zip(x, y, yhat, error):
    ax.plot([xi, xi], [yi, yhi], linestyle="--", color="black")
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xi, min(yi, yhi)), ei, ei, color="red", alpha=0.3))
ax.set_xlabel("Head Circumference (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Age (weeks)")
ax.set_title(f"MSE = {round(mse, 2)}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

$$\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \frac{1}{4} \Bigl[ (-0.3)^2 + 0^2 + 0.5^2 + (-0.2)^2 \Bigr] = 0.09.$$

::: footer
$\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = 0.38$.
:::

## Sensitive to outliers

$$
\text{If we instead had }
    \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}

```{python}
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((xi, min(yi, yhi)), ei, ei, color="red", alpha=0.3))
ax.set_xlabel("Head Circumference (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Age (weeks)")
ax.set_title(f"MSE = {round(mse, 2)}")
```

## Multiple Linear Regression (MLR)

Scenario: use _temperature ($^\circ C$)_ **and** _humidity (%)_ to predict _rainfall (mm)_

$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    27 & 80 \\
    32 & 70 \\
    28 & 72 \\
    22 & 86 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    6 \\
    7 \\
    6 \\
    4 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    5.7 \\
    7.2 \\
    5.9 \\
    4.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$\hat{y}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p = \beta_0 + \left \langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \right \rangle$$

```{python}
weather = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [27, 32, 28, 22], "humidity": [80, 70, 72, 86]})
rainfall = np.array([6, 7, 6, 4])
model = LinearRegression().fit(weather, rainfall)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.4f}, Coefficients: {model.coef_}")
model.predict(weather)
```

## MLR's design matrix

Scenario: use _temperature ($^\circ C$)_ **and** _humidity (%)_ to predict _rainfall (mm)_

$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 27 & 80 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 32 & 70 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 28 & 72 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 22 & 86 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    6 \\
    7 \\
    6 \\
    4 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    5.7 \\
    7.2 \\
    5.9 \\
    4.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$\hat{y}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \beta_0 x_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p = \langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle$$

::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{python}
weather.to_numpy()
```

:::
::: {.column width="70%"}
```{python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(weather)), weather.to_numpy()])
X
```

:::
:::

## MLR is just matrix equations

$$
  \boldsymbol{\beta} = (\boldsymbol{X}^\top\boldsymbol{X})^{-1} \boldsymbol{X}^\top \boldsymbol{y}
$$

::: columns
::: column
```{python}
model = LinearRegression().fit(
    weather, rainfall)
np.concatenate(
    [[model.intercept_], model.coef_])
```
:::
::: column
```{python}
y = rainfall
beta = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)
beta
```
:::
:::

$$
  \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

::: columns
::: column
```{python}
model.predict(weather)
```
:::
::: column
```{python}
X @ beta
```
:::
:::

## MLR after normalising the inputs

Scenario: use _temperature ($z$-score)_ **and** _humidity ($z$-score)_ to predict _rainfall (mm)_
$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & -0.06 & 0.41 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 1.15 & -0.95 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0.18 & -0.68 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & -1.28 & 1.22 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    6 \\
    7 \\
    6 \\
    4 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    5.7 \\
    7.2 \\
    5.9 \\
    4.2 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$\hat{y}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \beta_0 x_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_p x_p = \langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle$$

```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

weather = pd.DataFrame({"temperature": [27, 32, 28, 22], "humidity": [80, 70, 72, 86]})
scaler = StandardScaler()
weather_sc = pd.DataFrame(scaler.fit_transform(weather), columns=weather.columns)
rainfall = np.array([6, 7, 6, 4])
model = LinearRegression().fit(weather_sc, rainfall)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.4f}, Coefficients: {model.coef_}")
model.predict(weather_sc)
```

## SLR with categorical inputs

Scenario: use _property type_ to predict its _sale price ($)_

$$
\boldsymbol{x} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{red}{\text{Unit}} \\
    \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}} \\
    \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}} \\
    \textcolor{blue}{\text{House}} \\
\end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 1 & 0 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0 & 1 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0 & 1 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0 & 0 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    300000 \\
    500000 \\
    510000 \\
    700000 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    300000 \\
    505000 \\
    505000 \\
    700000 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\hat{y}(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \underbrace{I(x = \textcolor{red}{\text{Unit}})}_{=: x_1} + \beta_2 \underbrace{I(x = \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}})}_{=: x_2} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
$$

```{python}
property_type = pd.Categorical(["Unit", "TownHouse", "TownHouse", "House"])
price = np.array([300000, 500000, 510000, 700000])
X = pd.get_dummies(property_type, drop_first=True, dtype=int)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, price)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.2f}, Coefficients: {dict(zip(X.columns, model.coef_))}")
model.predict(X)
```

## Changing the base case

Scenario: use _property type_ to predict its _sale price ($)_

$$
\boldsymbol{x} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{red}{\text{Unit}} \\
    \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}} \\
    \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}} \\
    \textcolor{blue}{\text{House}} \\
\end{pmatrix} \longrightarrow \boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0 & 0 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 1 & 0 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 1 & 0 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 0 & 1 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    300000 \\
    500000 \\
    510000 \\
    700000 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    300000 \\
    505000 \\
    505000 \\
    700000 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

$$
\hat{y}(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \underbrace{I(x = \textcolor{green}{\text{TownHouse}})}_{=: x_1} + \beta_2 \underbrace{I(x = \textcolor{blue}{\text{House}})}_{=: x_2} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
$$

```{python}
property_type = pd.Categorical(
    ["Unit", "TownHouse", "TownHouse", "House"],
    categories=["Unit", "TownHouse", "House"],
)
price = np.array([300000, 500000, 510000, 700000])
X = pd.get_dummies(property_type, drop_first=True, dtype=int)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, price)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.2f}, Coefficients: {dict(zip(X.columns, model.coef_))}")
model.predict(X)
```

$$


## Dates as categorical inputs

Imagine you had dataset with 157,209 rows and one covariate column was 'date of birth'.
There were 27,485 unique values for the date of birth column.
You make a linear regression with the date of birth as an input, and treat it as a categorical variable.

::: {.fragment}
Pandas/sklearn would make a design matrix of size $157,209 \times 27,485$.
This has 4,320,889,365 numbers in it.
Each number is stored as 8 bytes, so the matrix is roughly
$$
34,000,000,000 \text{ bytes}
= 34,000,000 \text{ KB}
= 34,000 \text{ MB}
= 34 \text{ GB}.
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Question:** How do we avoid this situation of crashing our computer with an 'out of memory' error?
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Solution:** Don't train on the date of birth --- at least, not as a categorical variable.
Turn it into a numerical variable, e.g. age.
If the date column were not 'date of birth', maybe calculate the number of days since some reference date, or split into day, month, year columns.
:::


# Generalised Linear Models Recap

## MLR with categorical targets

Scenario: use _tumour radius (mm)_ and _ages (years)_ to predict _benign_ **or** _malignant_
$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 14.8 & 48 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 16.4 & 49 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 15.5 & 47 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 14.2 & 46 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \text{Benign} \\
    \text{Malignant} \\
    \text{Benign} \\
    \text{Malignant} \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    ? \\
    ? \\
    ? \\
    ? \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Step 1: Make a linear prediction
$$ \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p , \quad \text{a.k.a.} \quad \langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle.$$
:::
::: {.fragment}
Step 2: Shove it through some function to make it a probability $$\sigma(\langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle)$$
Interpret that as being the probability of the positive class.
:::
::: {.fragment}
Step 3: Make a decision based on that probability. E.g., if the probability is greater than 0.5, predict the positive class.
:::

## Binomial regression

Scenario: use _tumour radius (mm)_ and _ages (years)_ to predict _benign_ **or** _malignant_
$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 14.8 & 48 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 16.4 & 49 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 15.5 & 47 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 14.2 & 46 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}
    -0.46 \\
    0.18 \\
    0.37 \\
    -0.09 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

df = pd.DataFrame({"radius": [14.8, 16.4, 15.5, 14.2], "age": [48, 49, 47, 46]})
tumour = np.array(["Benign", "Malignant", "Benign", "Malignant"])
model = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(df, tumour)
```

Step 1: Make a linear prediction

```{python}
linear = model.decision_function(df)
linear
```

```{python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(df)), df.to_numpy()])
beta = np.concatenate([model.intercept_, model.coef_.flatten()])
X @ beta
```

## Logistic regression and probit regression

::: columns
::: column

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

x = np.arange(-6, 6, 0.1)
y = sigmoid(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.plot(x, y, linewidth=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("Sigmoid function")
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
plt.show()
```

This give you **logistic regression**.
:::
::: column

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 5
from scipy.stats import norm

x = np.arange(-6, 6, 0.1)
y = norm.cdf(x)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.plot(x, y, linewidth=1.5)
ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.set_ylabel("y")
ax.set_title("Normal CDF function")
ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="box")
plt.show()
```

This gives you **probit regression**.
:::
:::

## Logistic Regression

Scenario: use _tumour radius (mm)_ and _ages (years)_ to predict _benign_ **or** _malignant_
$$
\boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}
    -0.46 \\
    0.18 \\
    0.37 \\
    -0.09 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma( \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} ) = \begin{pmatrix}
    39\% \\
    55\% \\
    59\% \\
    48\% \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

```{python}
df = pd.DataFrame({"radius": [14.8, 16.4, 15.5, 14.2], "age": [48, 49, 47, 46]})
tumour = np.array(["Benign", "Malignant", "Benign", "Malignant"])
model = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(df, tumour)
```

Step 2: Shove it through some function to make it a probability

```{python}
sigmoid(linear)
```

```{python}
# Probability of the positive class (Malignant)
model.predict_proba(df)[:, 1]
```

## Predicting categories

Scenario: use _tumour radius (mm)_ and _ages (years)_ to predict _benign_ **or** _malignant_
$$
\boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \text{Benign} \\
    \textbf{\text{Malignant}} \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \sigma( \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} ) = \begin{pmatrix}
    39\% \\
    55\% \\
    59\% \\
    48\% \\
\end{pmatrix} , \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \text{Benign} \\
    \text{Malignant} \\
    \text{Malignant} \\
    \text{Benign} \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

```{python}
df = pd.DataFrame({"radius": [14.8, 16.4, 15.5, 14.2], "age": [48, 49, 47, 46]})
tumour = np.array(["Benign", "Malignant", "Benign", "Malignant"])
model = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(df, tumour)
```

```{python}
predict_probs = model.predict_proba(df)[:, 1]
print(np.round(100 * predict_probs, 2))
cutoff = 0.5
predicted_tumours = np.where(predict_probs > cutoff, "Malignant", "Benign")
print(predicted_tumours)
```

## Assessing accuracy in classification problems

Scenario: use _tumour radius (mm)_ and _ages (years)_ to predict _benign_ **or** _malignant_
$$
\boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{Green}{\text{Benign}} \\
    \textcolor{Green}{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \textcolor{Red}{\text{Benign}} \\
    \textcolor{Red}{\text{Malignant}} \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{Green}{\text{Benign}} \\
    \textcolor{Green}{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \textcolor{Red}{\text{Malignant}} \\
    \textcolor{Red}{\text{Benign}} \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

::: columns
::: column
Accuracy: $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n I(y_i = \hat{y}_i)$$
:::
::: column
Error rate: $$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n I(y_i \neq \hat{y}_i)$$
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
The word "accuracy" is used often used loosely when discussing models, particularly regression models.
In the context of classification it has this specific meaning.
:::

## Poisson regression

Scenario: use _population density_ to predict the daily **count of** _gun violence incidents_

$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 10 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 15 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 12 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 18 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    155 \\
    208 \\
    116 \\
    301 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{y}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    ? \\
    ? \\
    ? \\
    ? \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Step 1: Make a linear prediction
$$ \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p , \quad \text{a.k.a.} \quad \langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle.$$
:::
::: {.fragment}
Step 2: Shove it through some function to make it positive $$\exp(\langle \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{x} \rangle)$$
Interpret that as being the expected count.
:::

## Predict the mean of a Poisson distribution

Scenario: use _population density_ to predict the daily **count of** _gun violence incidents_

$$
\boldsymbol{X} = \begin{pmatrix}
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 10 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 15 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 12 \\
    \textcolor{grey}{1} & 18 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{y} = \begin{pmatrix}
    155 \\
    208 \\
    116 \\
    301 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta} = \begin{pmatrix}
    4.82 \\
    5.35 \\
    5.03 \\
    5.67 \\
\end{pmatrix}, \quad \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} = \begin{pmatrix}
    125.1 \\
    211.3 \\
    154.3 \\
    289.4 \\
\end{pmatrix}
$$

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor

guns = pd.DataFrame({"density": [10, 15, 12, 18]})
incidents = np.array([155, 208, 116, 301])
model = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0).fit(guns, incidents)
print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.4f}, Coefficients: {model.coef_}")

# Link (linear predictor)
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(guns)), guns.to_numpy()])
beta = np.concatenate([[model.intercept_], model.coef_])
linear = X @ beta
linear

# Response (expected count)
model.predict(guns)
```

## Trees

```{python}
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree

df = pd.DataFrame({"radius": [14.8, 16.4, 15.5, 14.2], "age": [48, 49, 47, 46]})
tumour = np.array(["Benign", "Malignant", "Benign", "Malignant"])
model = DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_split=2).fit(df, tumour)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
plot_tree(model, feature_names=list(df.columns), class_names=model.classes_, filled=True, ax=ax)
plt.show()
```
